item.title: LitUbik: open-source software for human-led systematic reviews with traceable AI assistance
item.description: arXiv:2610.37181v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LitUbik is an open-source, self-hosted tool for conducting systematic reviews, from the registered protocol to the PRISMA 2020 diagram. LitUbik covers calibrated search equations, automated searching, deduplication, blinded multi-reviewer screening, full-text retrieval, snowballing, appraisal, extraction and reporting, on one server or across disconnected instances. At each stage, optional AI assistance from commercial or local language models offers proposals that a named reviewer accepts or rejects. Every AI call is logged, so the AI-use disclosure is written from a record. A systematic review of 31 papers on review tools, conducted in LitUbik, compares it with existing tools and illustrates its use. LitUbik is distributed under AGPLv3.
item.dc:creator: Adolphe J. Bequet, Sebastien Laurent, Baptiste Bouvier

item.title: Jaxnasium: Embracing PyTrees For Any-Agent, Cross-Suite Reinforcement Learning
item.description: arXiv:2610.36075v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Hardware-accelerated reinforcement learning in JAX has gained rapid popularity in recent years and has proven to be a successful method of scaling online reinforcement learning. The resulting ecosystem, however, is fragmented: environment suites define their own interfaces, and algorithm implementations are typically written for a single suite, a single type of space, and either JAX-native or host-based environments. Here we present Jaxnasium, a library for JAX-based reinforcement learning, aiming to make the field more accessible. Jaxnasium represents observation and action spaces as PyTrees, and uses this structure to build networks and support multi-agent processing. Through this, its near-single-file implementations run on discrete, continuous, image, and composite spaces, as well as in multi-agent environments, without any changes to the algorithm code. The same files serve as readable, research-friendly algorithms, as well as importable algorithms for more applied workloads. Through a minimal Gymnasium-style interface and wrappers for 11 suites, over 300 environments are available on which a small PPO implementation with default hyperparameters is able to run. Additionally, through a simple wrapper, we can run Gymnasium and EnvPool environments with the same algorithm and training loop, with no performance loss compared to architectures specifically built for training JAX algorithms on host-based environments. Jaxnasium further provides tools for multi-seed evaluation, hyperparameter sweeps, and project scaffolding. Jaxnasium is open-sourced at https://github.com/ponseko/jaxnasium
item.dc:creator: Koen Ponse, Aske Plaat, Thomas M. Moerland

item.title: Organizational Structure and the Research of U.S. Library and Information Science Schools
item.description: arXiv:2601.20806v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: U.S. Library and Information Science (LIS) schools are organized differently: some are independent, and others share a parent unit with computing, communication, education, or the arts and sciences. We ask whether their research differs accordingly, using 18,048 publications (2013--2026) by 1,602 faculty members at 44 ALA-accredited schools. We grouped the 15,934 publications with abstracts into 15 research themes with document embeddings and hierarchical clustering, and classified venues by field. Faculty members' research profiles differ by school type in themes and, more clearly, in venues, but type accounts for only 2.2% and 5.3% of the variation; most lies among faculty of the same school. The differences run from libraries and archives to computational research. Schools housed with computing spread over the most themes and publish most on security, networks, and urban computing, on clinical and biomedical informatics, and in computer science venues; schools housed with education spread over the fewest and concentrate most on libraries, archives, and computing education; independent schools stay closest to the average. Over the period, schools moved away from library research and LIS venues, but seldom toward the venues of their parent unit's discipline. Research appears to follow a school's faculty more than its parent unit.
item.dc:creator: Jiangen He, Wen Lou

item.title: More of the same? Are scientific papers losing originality?
item.description: arXiv:2609.32963v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Scientific output is growing rapidly, but it is unclear whether the expanding literature remains original or is increasingly repeating itself. Originality has many dimensions. One dimension can now be measured directly: how textually distinct a paper is from the work that came before it. Using semantic language models, we screened more than 26,000 full-text papers across eight fields in the CORE database (2015--2025) for passages resembling recent literature. We compared every paper against a fixed-size sample of earlier work, so increases in resemblance are not a by-product of literature growth. We find that the share of a paper's text resembling recent work was stable before 2021, then rose sharply, more than tripling by 2025. The increase came not from a few papers borrowing more heavily but from resemblance spreading across the literature: more papers now contain passages that echo recent work, and almost none of this growth is explained by cited work. We also found an analogous increase in passages expressing the same scientific idea. The pattern held across robustness checks and replicated in a second, independent database. Along this one measurable axis of originality, scientific writing has become less distinct from the work preceding it.
item.dc:creator: Ilan Doron-Arad, Elchanan Mossel

item.title: Streamlining and standardizing software citations with The Software Citation Station
item.description: arXiv:2406.04405v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Software is crucial for the advancement of science, especially in the context of rapidly growing datasets that increasingly require algorithm and pipeline development to process data and produce results. However, software has not always been consistently cited, despite the importance of citations in strengthening support for software development. To encourage, streamline, and standardize the process of citing software in academic works, we introduce 'The Software Citation Station': a publicly available website and tool to quickly find correct software citation statements and add them to publications.
item.dc:creator: Tom Wagg, Floor S. Broekgaarden, Phil R. Van-Lane
